title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 30: Rufino v. Endriga: Does the President Have the Power to Appoint CCP Trustees?
keywords: heads of departments, agencies, commissions or boards
primary_topics: Chapter 30 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Rufino v. Endriga, in which the Court by a vote of 10-3 held Section 6 (b and c) of Presidential Decree No. 15 irreconcilable with Section 16 of Article VII of the Constitution, because it let CCP trustees elect fellow trustees equal to them in rank.

The textual holding on the word 'heads': Section 16 authorizes Congress to vest the appointing power in the heads of departments, agencies, commissions or boards -- meaning their chairpersons, not their members -- so only the CCP board chairperson could be given the power to appoint lower-ranked CCP officers.

The control holding: the CCP falls under the Executive Branch and thus under the President's power of control, and a provision letting the trustees fill their own vacancies made the CCP a self-perpetuating entity virtually outside that control, which no public office may be under the present Constitution.

The Dissent of Justice Tinga, who argued that the board as a collegial body outranks its individual members, that the Appointments clause allowed Congress to vest the power in it, and that executive control does not authorize removing officials whose terms are fixed by law.
sub_topics: The Endriga group had been appointed to the CCP board by President Fidel V. Ramos in 1995 with appointments extending only until December 31, 1998, and on December 22, 1998 President Joseph Estrada advised them that they were being replaced by seven new appointees led by Armita B. Rufino.

Dislodged from the CCP, Endriga filed quo warranto proceedings questioning the President's authority to appoint new board members, invoking Section 6(b) of PD 15, under which vacancies 'shall be filled by election by a vote of a majority of the trustees' and the President may act only when the board is entirely vacant.

With ten incumbent trustees still holding office and only one seat vacant, the Endriga group argued that presidential appointment was unjustified because the board itself had the statutory power to fill any vacancy by election.

On May 14, 1999 the Court of Appeals granted the quo warranto Petition, declared the Endriga group lawfully entitled to office and ousted the respondents, holding that the President could appoint only when the board was entirely vacant.

On appeal the Rufino group asserted that Section 6(b) was unconstitutional for being repugnant to Section 16 of Article VII, which allows the appointment only of officers lower in rank than the appointing power, and the lone issue became the constitutionality of Section 6 (b and c).

A supervening event -- the resignation of the Rufino group and the appointment of new trustees by President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo -- could have mooted the case, but the Court passed on the merits to prevent a repeat of the controversy and to protect the CCP from being periodically wracked by internecine politics, brushing aside procedural barriers given the importance of the issues.

By 10-3 the Court held that Section 6 (b) authorizes the appointing officer to appoint an officer equal in rank to himself, a situation the constitutional grant -- restricted to officers lower in rank -- clearly excludes.

The Court then held that the word 'heads' in Section 16 refers to chairpersons rather than members, for three reasons: past and present Constitutions used different phrasing ('in the courts', 'the Supreme Court', 'members of the Cabinet', 'the Constitutional Commissions') whenever the power was granted to the members of a collegial body; the deliberations show the phrase was an enumeration of offices whose heads may be vested with the power; and every commission or board has a chief executive who is its head.

Since Section 8 of PD 15 and Section 3 of the CCP's Revised Rules and Regulations recognized the board chairperson as head of the CCP with power to appoint, remove and discipline its officers and personnel, the chairperson was the only officer who could be vested by law with the power to appoint lower-ranked CCP officers.

Section 6 (b and c) was also found to run afoul of the President's power of control under Section 17 of Article VII, since under the Revised Administrative Code any agency not placed under a specific department falls under the Office of the President, and the CCP -- neither legislative, judicial, independent constitutional, quasi-judicial nor a local government unit -- necessarily fell under the Executive Branch.

By letting the trustees fill vacancies, the provision insulated the CCP from political influence and pressure, particularly from the President, making it a self-perpetuating entity that could not legally exist under the present Constitution; the CCP's autonomy of policy and operation did not free it from presidential control.

Justice Tinga dissented, warning that the majority had expanded executive control so far as to let the President make all appointments in the Executive Branch, diminishing the congressional power in the Appointments clause and rendering it inutile.

He argued that the board of trustees as a body was the head of the CCP and superior in rank to any individual trustee, citing GMCR v. Bell Telecommunications for the proposition that collegiate bodies outrank any individual member, even the presiding officer -- so electing fellow trustees was not appointing officers of equal rank.

He further noted that the respondents' statutory four-year term had not expired when President Estrada advised them of their replacements, so the majority sanctioned the removal of officials whose terms were fixed by law -- something executive control cannot justify, since the President must ensure that the laws be faithfully executed.

Citing Ang-Angco v. Castillo, he stressed that executive control applies to the acts of a subordinate and not to the actor himself, that the fixity of terms destroys the power of removal at pleasure, and that removal without legal cause was unconstitutional and contrary to Civil Service laws guaranteeing security of tenure.

Finally he discerned a clash between executive control and the prerogative of Congress to legislate eligibility requirements and terms of office, faulting the majority for allowing the President to ignore or countermand statutory limitations in the charters of GOCCs like the CCP.

notable_anecdotes: The controversy had the shape of a palace succession: trustees named by President Ramos in 1995 were told by President Estrada on December 22, 1998 that seven new appointees would take their places.

With only one seat actually vacant and ten trustees still in office, the ousted group argued that the board -- not the President -- had the statutory power to fill it, and won in the Court of Appeals.
By the time the case reached judgment the Rufino group had resigned and President Arroyo had named still another set of trustees, so the Court decided a dispute that had already changed casts twice.
The Court said plainly why it would not dismiss the case as moot: to keep the CCP from being periodically wracked by internecine politics.
The Dissent turned the majority's own vocabulary against it, arguing that the board of trustees as a body was itself the 'head' of the CCP and therefore superior to any single trustee it might elect.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 30 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Rufino v. Endriga, the quarrel over who may name the trustees of the Cultural Center of the Philippines. Trustees appointed by President Fidel V. Ramos in 1995, whose terms ran to December 31, 1998, were told by President Joseph Estrada on December 22, 1998 that seven new appointees led by Armita B. Rufino would replace them; the ousted Endriga group filed quo warranto, invoking Section 6(b) of Presidential Decree 15, under which the remaining trustees fill vacancies by election and the President may act only when the board is entirely vacant. The Court of Appeals granted the Petition, and on appeal the Rufino group attacked Section 6(b) as repugnant to Section 16 of Article VII, which allows the appointment only of officers lower in rank. Although the Rufino group's resignation and President Arroyo's appointment of new trustees could have mooted the case, the Court passed on the merits to prevent a repeat of the controversy and to protect the CCP from being periodically wracked by internecine politics. By 10-3 it held Section 6 (b and c) irreconcilable with the Constitution, since it authorized an appointing officer to appoint an officer equal in rank to himself. It then held that the word 'heads' in Section 16 refers to the chairpersons of commissions or boards and not to their members, reasoning from the different phrasing used in the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions when the power was granted to members of a collegial body, from the framers' deliberations, and from the fact that every board has a chief executive; since the CCP charter and rules made the board chairperson the head of the CCP, only the chairperson could be vested with the power to appoint lower-ranked officers. The provision also ran afoul of the President's power of control, for the CCP fell under the Executive Branch and the self-election of trustees made it a self-perpetuating entity virtually outside that control. Justice Tinga dissented, arguing that the board as a collegial body outranks its individual members, that the Appointments clause permitted Congress to vest the power in it, and that executive control reaches the acts of a subordinate and not the actor himself, so officials whose terms are fixed by law cannot be removed at the President's pleasure.
